claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state under standard synthesis conditions.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen are present in standard-processed Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen mediate local solute segregation in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 during cooling and thermal exposure.
Impurity-mediated segregation destabilizes the high-temperature BCC state of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Impurity-mediated segregation promotes nucleation of secondary phases in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Aging from several hundred degrees Celsius to near the BCC stability limit provides kinetically active diffusion of the interstitial impurities.
Slow cooling and aging permit sufficient impurity segregation for the proposed mechanism to operate.
Rapid quenching suppresses impurity diffusion enough to make the proposed mechanism irrelevant.
Localized oxygen- or nitrogen-enriched regions induce compositional heterogeneity.
Impurity segregation creates compositional gradients that reduce local BCC stability.
The impurity-induced compositional gradients lower the energy barrier for secondary-phase nucleation.
The proposed impurity-driven process produces a multiphase microstructure.
In a Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory high-entropy alloy aged at 700 degrees Celsius, trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation.
In that refractory high-entropy alloy, depletion of interstitial solutes from the matrix accompanies progressive age softening.
Ultra-high-purity Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 should largely retain its BCC structure with minimal secondary-phase formation.
Oxygen- and nitrogen-doped samples should develop more secondary-phase precipitates and a more multiphase microstructure than ultra-high-purity samples under the same thermal exposure.
Local oxygen or nitrogen enrichment should spatially correlate with secondary-phase nucleation.
Below a critical impurity concentration, the BCC phase should remain metastably intact.
Standard processing minimizes but does not completely eliminate interstitial impurities in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
